title: Antibiotic resistance rises: 55% of samples in national surveillance resist several drugs, 93% in ICUs
excerpt: IEDCR's national AMR surveillance of 99,867 samples found multidrug resistance up nine points in a year. Three-quarters of antibiotics used were 'Watch' drugs.
content:
More than half of the bacterial samples tested in Bangladesh's latest national antimicrobial resistance (AMR) surveillance were resistant to several antibiotics, up from under half a year earlier, the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR) said on Wednesday (25 November), The Daily Star reported.

The surveillance covered 99,867 samples collected between July 2025 and June 2026. It found multidrug-resistant (MDR) bacteria in 55% of all samples, up from 46% in last year's report. In intensive care units (ICUs) the share rose from 89% to 93%. The findings were presented at IEDCR's Mohakhali office a day after World AMR Awareness Week ended.

According to the report, 795 of the 1,118 drug-bacteria combinations tested (71%) were in the "red zone", meaning the antibiotic worked against 60% of samples or fewer. The share was 90% in ICUs and 93% for blood samples from ICU patients. Zakir Hossain Habib, IEDCR's chief scientific officer, said E. coli (33%) and K. pneumoniae (21%) were again the most common bacteria. MDR in E. coli rose from 62.8% in 2022 to 69.3% in 2026, and in K. pneumoniae from 57.6% to 69.1%.

Some hospital bacteria were resistant to almost all available antibiotics: 49.3% of Acinetobacter samples and 30.6% of Pseudomonas aeruginosa samples were classed as extensively drug-resistant. The data came from 13 hospitals and 27 laboratories.

Use of antibiotics was also skewed. Under the World Health Organization's grouping, "Watch" antibiotics made up 75.3% of all use at the surveillance sites and first-line "Access" antibiotics only 16%. Third-generation cephalosporins, which have largely lost their effect, were still the most used. Some last-resort "Reserve" drugs such as linezolid were being given to outpatients, Habib said.

IEDCR recommended making AMR control a top priority, counting deaths from sepsis caused by MDR bacteria as AMR deaths, written justification for antibiotic prescriptions, a review of treatment after 48 hours, an end to over-the-counter antibiotic sales and e-prescriptions. Zahid Raihan, additional director general of the health directorate, said 60–70% of antibiotic prescriptions were written by people with no medical degree. State Minister for Health MA Muhit said AMR surveillance would be made a permanent part of the health system and called for joint work by the health, agriculture, livestock, fisheries, environment and food ministries.

Why it matters

Resistance makes common infections harder and costlier to treat, and hits poor patients who buy antibiotics without a prescription from pharmacies. NGOs running clinics, community health workers and pharmacy outreach can play a part in safer prescribing, finishing courses and infection control. Livestock and fisheries programmes also matter, as farm use of antibiotics is one of the drivers named by experts.

What to watch

  • Whether the health ministry acts on the prescription audit and over-the-counter sales ban that IEDCR recommended.
  • Publication of the full surveillance report and site-level antibiograms.
  • Whether AMR-linked deaths start being counted in official health data.
